qs.q: If x + 1/x = 4, find x² + 1/x².
qs.h: §1, the x + 1/x family, first link.

qs.q: If x − 1/x = 3 and x > 0, then x + 1/x =
qs.h: §1, the last line of the x + 1/x family — the two squares differ by 4.
qs.s: (x + 1/x)² = (x − 1/x)² + 4 = 9 + 4 = 13. Since x > 0, x + 1/x is positive, so it equals √13.

qs.q: If x + 1/x = 3, find x⁴ + 1/x⁴.
qs.h: §1 — go one link at a time; you cannot jump from x + 1/x to x⁴ + 1/x⁴ directly.

qs.q: If a + b = 7 and ab = 10, then a³ + b³ =
qs.h: §1, the rearranged cube identity (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b).

qs.q: If x² − 5x + 1 = 0, find x³ + 1/x³.
qs.h: §1 + §2 — divide the whole equation by x before you do anything else.

qs.q: If α and β are the roots of x² − 7x + 12 = 0, then α² + β² =
qs.h: §2, sum/product of roots and α² + β² = (α+β)² − 2αβ.

qs.q: If α and β are the roots of 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0, find 1/α + 1/β.
qs.h: §2, 1/α + 1/β = (α+β)/αβ. Don't find the roots.

qs.q: Find the maximum value of −2x² + 12x − 7.
qs.h: §2, Vertex — x = −b/2a. Do not differentiate.
qs.s: a = −2 < 0, so it has a maximum at x = −b/2a = −12/(−4) = 3. Value = −2(9) + 36 − 7 = 11.

qs.q: The equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots for
qs.h: §2, discriminant D = 0. Watch the sign — the trap in the options is dropping the negative root.
qs.s: Equal roots ⟹ D = k² − 4(1)(9) = 0 ⟹ k² = 36 ⟹ k = ±6. Both work; discarding −6 is the trap.

qs.q: For how many values of k are both roots of x² − 6x + k = 0 positive integers?
qs.h: §2, sum and product of roots. List the integer pairs summing to 6.
qs.s: Roots are positive integers summing to 6: (1,5), (2,4), (3,3). Products give k = 5, 8, 9 — three values.

qs.q: If a + b + c = 10 and ab + bc + ca = 31, find a² + b² + c².
qs.h: §1, (a + b + c)² identity — the converter between the two symmetric sums.

qs.q: If p, q, r are the roots of x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 = 0, then 1/p + 1/q + 1/r =
qs.h: §3, cubic coefficient relations. Write the target as (pq + qr + rp)/pqr.
qs.s: pq + qr + rp = c/a = 11 and pqr = −d/a = 6. So 1/p + 1/q + 1/r = 11/6.

qs.q: If a + b + c = 6, ab + bc + ca = 11 and abc = 6, find a³ + b³ + c³.
qs.h: §5, the workhorse identity used forwards — a³+b³+c³ = 3abc + (a+b+c)(Σa² − Σab).

qs.q: If a + b + c = 0, ab + bc + ca = −7 and abc = 6, find a⁴ + b⁴ + c⁴.
qs.h: §1 and §3 — first get Σa², then get Σa²b² from (Σab)² = Σa²b² + 2abc·Σa, then use (Σa²)² = Σa⁴ + 2Σa²b².
§4, Nested surds — find m + n = 9 and mn = 20.

qs.q: If √x + √y = 9 and √x − √y = 5, find x + y.
qs.h: §4, the sum-and-difference shortcut: x + y = (p² + q²)/2.

qs.q: If √(x + 9) + √x = 9, find x.
qs.h: §4, single-equation worked example — isolate one surd, square, then substitute back to check.

qs.q: If x = 1/(2 − √3), then x³ + 1/x³ =
qs.h: §4 — rationalise first, then notice the conjugate pair multiplies to 1, which puts you in §1's x + 1/x chain.

qs.q: If (3 + √5)/(3 − √5) = a + b√5 where a and b are rational, then a + b =
qs.h: §4, "compare parts" — rationalise, then match rational and irrational parts separately.

qs.q: Find the value of (5 − 8)³ + (8 − 11)³ + (11 − 5)³.
qs.h: §5, the recognition cue. Check what the three brackets add up to before expanding anything.
qs.s: Brackets are −3, −3, 6, which sum to 0. So the value = 3(−3)(−3)(6) = 162.

qs.q: If a + b + c = 0 and abc = 12, then a³ + b³ + c³ =
qs.h: §5, the one-line consequence of the workhorse identity.
qs.s: a + b + c = 0 ⟹ a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc = 36.

qs.q: Find the value of 7³ + 3³ − 10³.
qs.h: §5 — rewrite the third term as (−10)³ and check the sum of the three bases.
qs.s: Write as 7³ + 3³ + (−10)³. Bases sum to 0, so value = 3(7)(3)(−10) = −630.

qs.q: If a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc, which of the following must be true?
o: a + b + c = 0 or a = b = c
qs.h: §5, "The converse matters too" — and the Traps table.
qs.s: The identity gives (a+b+c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca) = 0. Either the first factor is 0, or the second is — and the second is zero exactly when a = b = c. Both cases are possible, so only (c) must be true.

qs.q: Find the minimum value of 9x + 4/x for x > 0.
qs.h: §6, AM ≥ GM applied to the two terms.

qs.h: §6, Modulus: |x| < a ⟺ −a < x < a.

qs.q: Two positive numbers have a sum of 20. Find their maximum possible product.
qs.h: §6, fixed sum ⟹ product is maximum when the terms are equal.
qs.s: Fixed sum ⟹ product maximal when equal: 10 × 10 = 100.

qs.q: The number of real values of x satisfying |x − 3| + |x + 2| = 5 is
qs.h: §6, case-split at every sign change — x = −2 and x = 3. Look carefully at the middle case.
qs.s: The two critical points are −2 and 3, whose distance is exactly 5. For any x with −2 ≤ x ≤ 3 the two distances add to 5, so every such x is a solution.

qs.q: If |x − 1| + |x − 4| = 7, find the sum of all values of x.
qs.h: §6 — three cases, and discard any solution that falls outside its own case's range.
qs.s: Case x < 1: (1−x) + (4−x) = 7 ⟹ x = −1 ✓ (lies in range). Case 1 ≤ x ≤ 4: gives 3 = 7, no solution. Case x > 4: (x−1) + (x−4) = 7 ⟹ x = 6 ✓. Sum = −1 + 6 = 5.

qs.q: If f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x², then f(g(2)) =
qs.h: §7, Composite — work from the inside out.

qs.q: If f(x) + 3f(1/x) = 4x for all x ≠ 0, find f(3).
qs.h: §7, the substitute-the-reciprocal move — put x = 3, then x = 1/3, and eliminate.

qs.q: If f(x) = (x − 1)/(x + 1), find f(f(f(f(f(2))))) — that is, f applied five times to 2.
qs.h: §7, Composite. Simplify f(f(x)) in general first; the pattern repeats faster than you'd expect.
qs.s: f(f(x)) = (−2/(x+1)) ÷ (2x/(x+1)) = −1/x. So f applied four times returns x. Five applications = one application: f(2) = 1/3.

qs.q: If 3x + 5y = 31 and 5x + 3y = 33, find x + y.
qs.h: §8, "the habit that saves time" — the question asks for x + y, so don't solve for x and y separately.

qs.h: §8 — add the two equations. You never need the individual prices.
